The payment stayed the same. Why did the mortgage balance rise?

Four charts separate a fixed cash payment from interest charged, principal reduction and the debt added when the payment no longer covers the modeled interest.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a fixed payment after a variable-rate change

Hypothetical monthly-compounding loan illustration, not a lender agreement or approval to capitalize interest. Annual quoted rates are divided by twelve. Interest is charged on opening monthly debt; the selected payment arrives at month-end. When payment is below interest, the shortfall is added to debt in this model. The alternative uses the same opening path, then the separately selected payment after the rate change. No fees, arrears charges, renewal, property tax, penalty or lender intervention is calculated. The illustrative trigger is payment × 12 ÷ debt at the change, and must not substitute for a contractual trigger rate.

The central idea

A stable payment is a cash-flow fact, not proof that debt is falling. Compare the payment with interest charged on the current balance and check the contract’s response to a shortfall.

01

Separate a fixed payment from a fixed interest rate

A variable-rate mortgage can have a payment amount that stays unchanged for a time. That does not hold the borrowing rate or the interest portion of the payment constant. If interest rises while the cash payment stays the same, less of that payment is available to reduce principal.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada explains trigger rates and negative amortization for variable-rate loans with fixed payments. Its guidance also directs borrowers to the agreement and their financial institution for the actual trigger and available options.

This tool is an invented loan ledger. It applies a selected capitalization rule to show the arithmetic of unpaid interest; it does not establish that a lender permits that behavior, how long it may continue, or what action an actual agreement requires.

02

Read the first twelve payments before the rate changes

The default starts with CAD 400,000 of debt, a 5% nominal annual rate compounded monthly and CAD 2,400 paid at each month-end. Interest is the opening monthly balance multiplied by the annual quoted rate divided by twelve.

The first month’s interest is about CAD 1,666.67. The rest of the CAD 2,400 payment reduces principal. After twelve payments, debt is about CAD 390,995.51, a reduction of about CAD 9,004.49 from the opening balance.

Both comparison paths use this same first year. The alternative payment is introduced only after the selected rate change. This keeps their debt balances identical at the moment the new rate begins, making the next month’s payment allocation directly comparable.

03

At the new rate, compare the interest charge with the cash paid

The selected nominal annual rate becomes 8% after twelve completed months, so month thirteen uses the new rate. Interest on the shared opening balance is about CAD 2,606.64.

The fixed-payment path still pays CAD 2,400. Its principal allocation is CAD 2,400 − CAD 2,606.64 = negative CAD 206.64. Under this model’s capitalization assumption, that shortfall is added to debt, which ends the month at about CAD 391,202.14.

The alternative pays CAD 3,200 after the change. Against the same first changed-month interest, it reduces principal by about CAD 593.36. This path needs CAD 800 more cash that month. The difference is a budget commitment as well as a debt result; the additional payment is not generated automatically by the calculation.

04

Understand the algebraic trigger without treating it as a lender quote

In this monthly-compounding model, the interest-only boundary occurs when opening debt × nominal annual rate ÷ 12 = monthly payment. Solving for the annual rate gives payment multiplied by twelve, divided by opening debt.

At the default balance immediately before the change, that illustrative boundary is about 7.3658% nominal annually. The selected 8% rate is above it, so the unchanged payment does not cover the modeled monthly interest. Exactly at the boundary, payment covers interest and contributes zero principal.

This result uses the entered balance and a specific compounding convention. A contract may use other timing, payment components or trigger provisions. Confirm its exact rate and response with the lender. The grid is an explanation of the relationship between rate, debt and payment, rather than a substitute for the agreement’s calculation.

05

Reconcile debt, cash payments and interest over the full window

Over sixty model months, the unchanged-payment path pays CAD 144,000 in cash and incurs about CAD 146,639.47 of interest charges. Its ending debt is therefore CAD 400,000 + CAD 146,639.47 − CAD 144,000 = CAD 402,639.47.

About CAD 11,643.96 of interest is added to debt during months when payment is below the charge. That amount is larger than the net increase from the original debt because the first year had already reduced principal. “Interest added” and “ending debt minus original debt” measure different things.

The alternative pays CAD 182,400 in cash, incurs about CAD 139,959.53 of interest and ends owing about CAD 357,559.53. Its larger cash commitment is CAD 38,400 over the window. The balance comparison does not invest cash retained by the fixed-payment path or value that liquidity; it is a loan-ledger comparison.

06

Use the matrix to identify the question that needs action

The matrix starts every cell with the same debt immediately before the change. Its rows replace the nominal annual rate, and its columns replace the monthly payment. A positive cell shows principal reduction in the first changed month. A negative cell shows interest that would be added under the illustrative rule.

The cumulative-interest chart reports charges, including amounts not paid in cash. Once added to the balance, those amounts can generate further interest in later periods. Calling the entire charge “interest paid” would hide that distinction.

The model has no fees, property-tax component, renewal, missed-payment penalty or lender intervention. Review those items separately, together with the cash needed for a changed payment or additional principal. The useful output is an explicit comparison: what cash is paid, what interest is charged, whether debt is reducing, and what the agreement requires if the current payment becomes insufficient.
